newsitem.title: USA: Governors oppose Clinton plan on Medicaid spending.
newsitem.headline: Governors oppose Clinton plan on Medicaid spending.

text.p: The National Governors' Association said Friday it would oppose any plan by President Clinton to clamp tight spending limits on the Medicaid programme for the poor, charging it would shift costs to the states.

The governors have drafted a resolution, which association officials expect to be adopted at their winter meeting beginning Saturday, opposing any cap on spending for the programme, which serves 37 million poor, elderly and disabled.
A bipartisan group of six governors wrote to Clinton and congressional leaders this week to outline the policy and ask the White House to consult closely with them on Medicaid.

"Any unilateral cap on the Medicaid programme will shift costs to state and local governments that they simply cannot afford," the governors' resolution said. "The governors adamantly oppose a cap on federal Medicaid spending in any form."
The resolution also asks policymakers to give states more flexibility to run Medicaid, including greater use of managed care and relief from some nursing home regulations.

Medicaid is one of a series of contentious issues the governors will address at their meeting. They want Congress to provide relief of a new welfare law ending federal aid to most legal immigrants and are worried about air quality standards.
Clinton was expected to propose annual limits on Medicaid spending as part of a balanced budget plan he will send to Congress next week, administration officials have said.

Medicaid is an open-ended entitlement, jointly funded by state and federal governments. The programme has been the fastest growing part of many state budgets, comprising about 20 percent of state spending on average. States spent about $70 billion on Medicaid last year.
"As we've said many times before, the per capita (Medicaid spending) cap is good policy," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters at the White House Friday.
An official of the Democratic Governors' Association played down the importance of the resolution, calling it "more a reiteration of existing policy than breaking new ground."
Liberal Democrats in Congress have said they will fight any Clinton plan to set limits on annual Medicaid growth, saying it could force states to cut services.
Poor children and the elderly make up the bulk of Medicaid recipients, but most of the money goes toward long-term care.
During the last session of Congress, Republicans proposed to give states control of Medicaid under a block grant. They are more receptive to the idea of capping spending.
"How do you reach a balanced budget without a cap?" said one Republican aide. But other Republican aides said there were a host of unanswered questions about the Clinton plan.

In their resolution, the governors warned the White House and Congress to be careful in any proposal to expand outreach to poor children under Medicaid. Recent studies estimate millions of poor children who are eligible for Medicaid are not receiving benefits. Clinton's budget is expected to suggest new ways to reach poor children.
"No Medicaid outreach strategy should create an opportunity for shifting private sector insurance efforts onto the public sector," the resolution said.
While the governors split with Clinton on Medicaid, they are closer regarding legal immigrants and the new welfare law.
The welfare law ends federal nutrition and disability aid to most legal immigrants. Governors say the law will impose a huge cost shift and want Congress to provide some relief.

Republican congressional leaders say they do not want to reopen the law. Clinton plans to propose about $16 billion in welfare "fixes" in his budget. Much of that money would be targeted at restoring aid to legal immigrants.
